purpose: Frozen external-validation benchmark registry. Every target, its population, its discrepancy measure, and its pass criterion are fixed here BEFORE the model outputs are compared against them. A benchmark whose criterion is written after seeing the comparison is not a validation.
governing_rules: No target in this registry was used to choose, tune, or fit any model parameter. Any target that was is marked used_for: calibration and is excluded from the validation verdict.
Failures are reported as results. The registry is not re-tuned until every benchmark passes; a model that fails an external check has told you something.
A benchmark the model is structurally incapable of addressing is recorded as not_addressable with the structural reason, rather than being quietly dropped or scored as a pass.
Construct match is stated per benchmark. Where the model's quantity and the target's quantity are not the same construct, the benchmark cannot be scored, however close the numbers look.

verdict_values.pass: the model's value falls within the target interval on the declared discrepancy measure
verdict_values.fail: the model's value falls outside it; reported, not corrected
verdict_values.not_addressable: the model has no output of this construct; the structural reason is given
verdict_values.not_scored: construct mismatch or an unresolved denominator makes a numeric comparison meaningless

benchmarks.name: Incident recovery-duration distribution
benchmarks.source: Neprash HT et al., JAMA Health Forum 2022
benchmarks.population: 374 publicly reported ransomware attacks on U.S. health care delivery organizations, 2016-2021. Not hospitals only.
benchmarks.model_endpoint: distribution of time to full clinical service restoration
benchmarks.uncertainty: Interval-censored. 67 events have known disruption of unknown duration and are excluded from the bins; that missingness is plausibly informative, since longer or more severe incidents may be less likely to have a cleanly reported end date.
benchmarks.direction: the model's recovery distribution should place non-negligible mass beyond one week
benchmarks.discrepancy_measure: duration-bin likelihood under the model's recovery distribution
benchmarks.structural_reason: The simulation horizon is 72 hours and the restoration rate implies a few-hundred-node estate recovers within hours once contained. The model cannot place ANY mass beyond one week, so it cannot be compared against a distribution whose mass is mostly beyond one week. This is a failure boundary of the current design, not a passing or failing score. Addressing it requires the layered recovery endpoints (72 h, 21 d, 90 d, 180 d tail) that the model specification requires and this version does not implement.

benchmarks.name: Attacked-hospital activity decline in the first week
benchmarks.source: Neprash H, McGlave C, Nikpay S, AEJ: Economic Policy 2026
benchmarks.population: U.S. hospitals with ransomware attacks, Medicare claims based
benchmarks.model_endpoint: reduction in delivered clinical service capacity during the first 7 days

target.units: proportional decline in volume during the first week

benchmarks.uncertainty: Point estimates by setting. Figures verified against the authors' working-paper text, which reports ER 16.7%, inpatient 25.4%, and outpatient 17-25%. The rebuild handoff summarised these as a single 17-24% range; the by-setting figures are used instead because they are what the source states. The published AEJ version should be re-checked before submission in case the estimates were revised in review.
benchmarks.discrepancy_measure: absolute difference between modeled week-1 activity loss and the target interval
benchmarks.structural_reason: Construct mismatch, and it is not a close one. The model reports weighted service-hours lost with binary per-step availability; the target is a change in patient volume. A hospital with a degraded but functioning EHR still admits patients, and the model has no representation of degraded operation, downtime procedures, or manual workarounds. Converting service-hours into volume would require exactly the patient-flow layer the model does not have. Reporting a number here would be manufacturing a validation.

citation_verification.method: authors' working-paper full text; the journal and PMC pages are behind automated-access challenges
citation_verification.discrepancy_found: the handoff's '17-24% in the first week' is narrower than, and not identical to, any single figure in the source

benchmarks.name: Return toward baseline volume over roughly three weeks
benchmarks.source: Neprash H, McGlave C, Nikpay S, AEJ: Economic Policy 2026
benchmarks.model_endpoint: time to return to full modeled clinical availability
benchmarks.uncertainty: The source states volume in all hospital settings recovers to pre-attack levels within two to three weeks. The handoff's 'approximately three weeks' is the upper end of that range.
benchmarks.direction: the modeled recovery time should be of the same order
benchmarks.discrepancy_measure: recovery-curve distance over the observation window
benchmarks.observed_model_behaviour: Technical recovery in the model completes far earlier than the observed three-week trajectory, and the horizon cannot represent the comparison window at all.
benchmarks.structural_reason: Same horizon limitation as recovery_duration_bins. This is recorded as a fail rather than not_addressable because the direction of the discrepancy is unambiguous and informative: the model recovers optimistically fast relative to the public record, and any decision read off its recovery objective inherits that optimism.

citation_verification.quote: Volume in all hospital settings recovers to pre-attack levels within two to three weeks.

benchmarks.name: ED visits and inpatient admissions at attacked California hospitals
benchmarks.model_endpoint: clinical service availability trajectory by week
benchmarks.uncertainty: point estimates from the published specification
benchmarks.structural_reason: Same construct mismatch as week_one_activity_loss, plus a horizon that ends before week 1 does.

benchmarks.name: Burden at emergency departments adjacent to an attacked hospital
benchmarks.source: Dameff C et al., JAMA Network Open 2023
benchmarks.population: one month-long U.S. attack and its neighboring EDs. A single regional case, not a national average.
benchmarks.direction: the model should produce demand displacement to neighboring facilities
benchmarks.structural_reason: The simulator runs exactly one facility per trial and has no representation of a neighboring hospital, patient transfer, or diversion. There is no output of this construct at any parameter setting. This is the single clearest statement of the model's scope limit.

benchmarks.name: Share of attacks affecting more than one hospital
benchmarks.source: Derived from the public THREAT hospital-linked file
benchmarks.population: 74 hospital-linked events, 149 deduplicated hospital-event records. Publicly reported and Medicare-linkable events only; not a probability sample.
benchmarks.model_endpoint: number of facilities affected per simulated incident
benchmarks.uncertainty: reporting-biased; a zero flag may mean not reported. See docs/evidence/THREAT_RECONCILIATION.md.
benchmarks.direction: the model should place non-zero mass on multi-facility incidents
benchmarks.observed_model_behaviour: The model places all mass on exactly one facility, against a target of 25.7% multi-hospital events with a maximum of 22.
benchmarks.structural_reason: A single-facility simulator cannot produce a multi-facility incident. Reported as an unambiguous fail rather than not_addressable because the target is directly comparable and the discrepancy is total: the model assigns probability zero to a quarter of the observed events.

benchmarks.name: Short-duration technical outage and recovery
benchmarks.source: Tully J et al., JAMA Network Open 2025
benchmarks.population: 2,232 hospitals with observable data during a non-malicious global update failure; 759 with detected disruption
benchmarks.model_endpoint: distribution of technical service outage duration
benchmarks.uncertainty: observational; classification of service outages varies
benchmarks.direction: two-sided, on the technical-recovery engine only
benchmarks.discrepancy_measure: median outage duration and the share recovered within six hours
benchmarks.scoring_note: This is the ONE benchmark the model's horizon can actually address, which is why it is scored numerically. It is a non-malicious update failure, so it validates the short-duration technical-restoration engine and nothing else. It is not a ransomware recovery distribution and must never be presented as one.

comparison.model_quantity: median longest continuous clinical service outage, and share of trials whose longest outage resolves within six hours, among trials in which any clinical service was disrupted

benchmarks.name: Share of attacks stopped before encryption
benchmarks.source: Sophos, The State of Ransomware in Healthcare 2025
benchmarks.population: self-reported healthcare ransomware victims across 17 countries, organizations of 100-5,000 employees
benchmarks.model_endpoint: share of trials contained before clinical service loss
benchmarks.uncertainty: vendor survey; self-selected respondents; not a probability sample of U.S. hospitals
benchmarks.discrepancy_measure: absolute difference in the contained-before-disruption share
benchmarks.scoring_note: Graded below administrative and peer-reviewed evidence, and reported as a loose consistency check rather than a target. A survey of victims across 17 countries and all organization sizes is not a U.S. hospital denominator. The comparison is informative only if the model is wildly outside the range.

comparison.model_quantity: share of trials with no clinical service outage exceeding the sustained-outage duration threshold, per profile

benchmarks.name: Hospital control adoption prevalence
benchmarks.source: HHS Hospital Cyber Resiliency Initiative: Landscape Analysis, 2023
benchmarks.population: CHIME data from 377 hospitals, a 59-organization Censinet/AHA/KLAS study, and 20 hospital interviews
benchmarks.uncertainty: survey-based; overlapping and partially self-reported samples
benchmarks.direction: the declared capacity profiles should span the observed range of postures
benchmarks.discrepancy_measure: qualitative coverage of the observed posture range
benchmarks.structural_reason: This is adoption prevalence, not control effectiveness, and it is used to argue that the three declared profiles span a plausible range of real postures. It is deliberately NOT used as an effect size, and it is not a validation target. It is listed here so that a reader can see it was used for scenario design and nothing else.
